Mr. Speaker, I have a sense that this House has heard a great deal on this Bill and has debated it and its companion legislation, Bill C-84, in considerable detail and at considerable length. I also have a sense that we have, occasionally, within the House of Commons, questions of morality which face us and on which we have to reflect our country.
They are often very difficult cases which, I am certain, are not popular. They are cases which, in the pre-election period, people may not want to confront. Yet, I think that in this case there is such a contradiction of everything which we as a country have stood for in terms of the protection of the individual under the due process of law, that this Bill simply becomes an unacceptable and, frankly, immoral imposition on the people of Canada.
I do not say that kind of thing about the trade legislation which I debate. That is an issue of economic and political choice. I disagree with the economic and political choice which is made. I think that the consequences of that choice are massive. I am prepared to debate it and we certainly have debated it in terms of questions, opposition days, and so forth.
The same is true with various of the privatizations which have come before this House. There have often, I think, been grievous mistakes for which future governments and future Canadians will end up having to pay. I think that is true, for instance, of the Air Canada legislation which was given second reading in this Parliament this week.
However, with this Bill we are dealing with something far more fundamental, something which cuts at the heart of our concept of the country much more than many of the other Bills which we have debated. I myself thought, frankly, that the Government, at some strategic point, would recognize that you cannot turn your back on hundreds of years of the building of due process of law within this country and within the countries from which many of us have come, whether Britain, France, or the hundreds of other countries from which we have come.
This is the final chance for the House of Commons to again consider again this legislation and pass judgment on what the Senate has suggested to us. This Bill still has as its fundamental purpose the effect of eliminating the potential for an independent hearing on the merits of the case of refugees who reach this country. Regardless of what the Senate may say, not only is it a negation of our traditional principles of fundamental justice, it is so un-Canadian that I cannot believe how the Government can continue along this path in spite of the opposition from so many groups to which we have looked for moral leadership in the past.
It is partly a personal consideration that I bring to bear when I look at a Bill like this. My grandparent's grandparents
June 10, 1988

came to Canada from Germany after the failed revolution of 1848. There was no question about admitting them to our country because they were not just refugees, they were refugees who had challenged an established regime. While they may not have been revolutionaries themselves, they certainly supported that democratic revolution and had to flee.
In 1988 or 1989, when the same kind of people come to this country, will they get the same kind of treatment that my grandparent's grandparents received? According to this Bill, there is absolutely no possibility that that will take place. I consider that a deeply unhappy blot on this Parliament, which was elected to try to bring change in our approach to the future.
Apart from my own family, I see this in my constituency where constituents have crossed from Eastern Europe, often at tremendous personal risk, and have been accepted here as refugees. I see others who have crossed from Central America, at great personal risk, and have had the right to a fair hearing in this country. That right is being eliminated by this Bill.
I say to the Minister who is shaking her head that the hearing which people will receive when they reach the border is not a hearing to consider the merits of their case. Because of that, it is not a full scale hearing before an independent body where they can put as much of a persuasive argument as possible that would allow some kind of assessment of their claim with justice and due process of justice being seen to have taken place.
I recognize the extreme pressures on the Government with respect to this issue. We are talking about a world in which there are millions of refugees whose dismal, difficult, dangerous position, whether it is in Thailand, Sudan or Latin America, is very much a blot on how the world community has operated.
I can see the pressures from the point of view of the Government to try to set up some kind of barriers that will somehow give us a handle on the great number of people in the world who want to be some place else because of the lack of democracy, lack of human rights, lack of equality within their own countries.
I understand as well the pressures brought to bear by the immigrant communities in my constituency who say that it is not right that someone claiming to be a refugee can stay here for five years before getting a hearing, go through various appeals and so on and ultimately be able stay in this country because of some sort of ministerial amnesty. They do not have as logical reason to be in this country as a relative of one of my constituents may have. There is a great sense of opposition and anger about that, which I must say that I share.
It is not right that governments in this country have so badly bungled the whole issue of refugees. The last two Governments in particular have simply been incapable of finding solutions that are both consistent with our traditions of natural law, of
Immigration Act, 1976
due process, of humanitarianism, and our tradition of fairness to existing immigrants in this country.
I think the particular amendments which have come before us are in fact amendments which improve the situation somewhat within a rather unfortunate Bill. The amendments from my colleague in the Liberal Party are amendments which make it much more of an independent process with respect to the determination of whether a refugee has a valid claim and makes absolutely certain that if a refugee is sent back to a third country, that third country admits the refugee and has a system in place which allows that refugee to have his or her claims determined fairly within that country.
The amendment which my Party colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), has added is, I think, crucial because it makes the point that our system has to include an assessment that recognizes the principles of fundamental justice. Chile may well have on its books, in print, a system in which the merits of refugee claims will be determined in Chile. We may well receive assurances that these people will be admitted to Chile, but all of us in this House, after some of our colleagues from all Parties have gone to Chile, surely know that we cannot trust that the principles of fundamental justice are in fact observed within that country. On that basis, it should not be possible, if the amendment from the Hon. Member for Spadina is accepted, to send a refugee back to Chile.
The same thing, I am certain, would be true in El Salvador, Guatemala or Honduras, countries about which I know something, and which do not reflect in their justice systems the principles of fundamental justice which are reflected by and large, with the exception of this Bill if it goes through, in our country.
For reasons which, frankly, are deeply personal, and for reasons which reflect the concerns of my constituents, we want to see a fair system to assess refugees, we want to get rid of this nonsense of massive amnesties periodically which simply indicates our system is not working properly. In the context of those kinds of concerns, I urge this House very strongly to adopt the amendment which has been brought forward as a subamendment by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina, and to subsequently adopt the amendments which have been moved by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). I think we will at least come closer, then, to seeing to it that there is not a completely black blot on the future of this country as it is looked at from around the world in terms of the due process of law which should be reflected in our refugee legislation.

I understand that since my grandparents and great grandparents came from much the same kind of background. However, he went on to say that the refugees today are the same as those in 1848, as if nothing has happened in the world since 1848 that would change the outlook or behavioural practices of people wanting to come to Canada.
Let me list just a few of the concepts which have now formed the behavioural patterns of people. For example, nihilism, which basically says it does not matter since nothing matters anyway. So you can do what you want. It is all a black future. There is no good consequence of anything, anyway, so go ahead and do what you want. There is existentialism, which makes everyone's individual outlook paramount. There is no uniform absolute. Nothing is clearly right or wrong. Therefore, the expression of your own particular authenticity is the most moral thing you can do. There is no absolute morality so it does not matter if you incite violence or peace in its own self. That is a very popular concept.
There is dialectical materialism. It began to be popular around 1848 but was not pervasive at that time. But for the last 150 years witness eastern Europe and the effect of dialectical materialism, where the state is supreme and individual rights are nothing. They have value only to the extent and to the degree they support the state. How about situational ethics, again where nothing is right or wrong except the situation in which you happen to be. It depends on the situation. Finally, the Marxist theology of Latin America which espouses violence for their cause. I want to remind the professor that when we have that cauldron of beliefs in the system, the thought forms of people coming to Canada have changed in the last 150 years, and Canada deserves some protection from people whose thoughts forms have changed, if they no longer hold to absolute rights and wrongs.
The Canadian people deserve the right to choose carefully on the basis of what is good for Canada as well as good for the refugee claimant in order that they can live in a sense of security and growing tolerance and understanding, but with the knowledge that the people who come here, come with some solid basis of understanding that there is a consensus in
Canada of what is right or wrong. We want them to share in that consensus.

He is a person who, presumably, holds a position of some responsibility, and should put the facts before Canadians in a truthful fashion, to put the facts before Canadians in a manner so that they will not be mislead and that does not play to the fears that some people may have.
For him even to suggest it, to use a figure of that nature, to talk about the whole population of the world and to suggest that somehow if we had a full hearing on the merits that there is the potential that all the people in the world would come to Canada indicates to me the kind of irresponsibility and demagogic fashion with which the Government has treated Canadians over the past year and a half since this Bill was introduced.
It reminds me of a definition or a quip that I read a week or two ago which said that a demagogue is someone who rocks the boat and then tries to convince everybody that there is a storm out there. This is exactly what the Government has been doing for the past 15 or 16 months. They have been trying to convince Canadians that there is a storm out there, that we Canadians have to protect ourselves or we will be flooded, deluged, with hundreds of thousands of people who will sweep over our borders.
I am reminded of a comment by Rabbi Gunther Plaut to the Canadian Council of Refugees at the meeting one year ago in which he noted how the Government uses language of this nature relating to climate, a wave, a deluge, the type of language which is designed to cull up some sense of a natural disaster or of something that is beyond the control of human beings in order to inspire or build up feelings of fear in people's minds.
I condemn in the strongest language this attitude. The Parliamentary Secretary continued that in comments he made just after the intervention of the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor (Mr. Langdon). He talked about Canadians deserving some protection from people who may incite violence. He talked about the changed circumstances since 1848. He talked about the kind of philosophies, dangerous philosophies presumably, that people hold these days. He said that Canadians deserve some protection and that we have the right to choose carefully, and the right to live with a sense of security. Again, Mr. Speaker, he was playing and pandering to the fears of Canadians in a fashion that can only be described as the height of irresponsibility.
Many things have changed since 1848. One of the things that has changed is the Geneva Convention of 1951, which is a significant deviation from the principle that existed before that convention, that a sovereign country had absolute control over who it permitted to enter its borders. The Geneva Convention

June 10, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
was implemented after the last world war. As we know, during that war hundreds of thousands of people became victims because they had nowhere to go. No country would accept them. It was felt necessary to provide individuals with the capacity to effect some salvation on their own, not to have to wait for the permission of a country, not to have to wait to be chosen by a consular official or an officer in an embassy, and not to have to stand in line in order to be patted on the head and told: "Yes, you can come to our country".
The idea and the fundamental revolution that was represented by the Geneva Convention was that somehow we were going to take away a little from the sovereignty of nations, that absolute sovereignty which said that a nation, a state alone controls its borders. We were going to allow people who regard themselves as refugees to move to a safe haven, to pack up and leave overnight, if necessary.
I gave the example in a letter to the papers, which I was fortunate to have published several weeks ago, of Billy Wilder, the famous film maker who received the Irving Thalberg Award at the Academy Awards this spring. He told the story of a consular official in a small Mexican border town where he had to go to apply for immigrant status and permanent residence after having been in the United States for six months. He talked about the trepidation that he felt when he went before this consular official. He came with very few documents. He came with perhaps his application form and one or two letters of reference. He presented this to the consular official who did not respond. There was what Wilder felt was an interminable period of silence. He decided to take his courage into his own hands and he explained that when he was told the Nazis were coming, he only had 15 minutes to pack a few things and leave. He did not have enough time to find his birth certificate, school records, or other documentation. These are the types of circumstances under which refugees have to leave.
The Geneva Convention was a significant change in international law in the sense that it provided individuals with the capacity to pack up and leave and to move to a safe haven without having to ask permission beforehand. The only obligation that states undertook under the Geneva Convention was not to refoule a refugee, not to turn back a person in need of protection, that is, states very jealously guard their sovereignty.
A state does not have to give a person permanent residence, citizenship, or a work permit. Under the Geneva Convention all the state obliges itself to do is not to send back a refugee. In order to implement that obligation, it is necessary for the state to have some procedure to determine whether the person is indeed a refugee, or is not a refugee, because refugees do not come with the word "refugee" stamped on their forehead. Yes, people make claims, some of which may be valid claims, and other claims may not be valid. A state has the obligation to examine the claim and have some procedure for determining whether indeed that person is or is not a refugee.
This whole debate is about refugee groups and people who work with refugees in this country and who have been arguing for a revision in our system for many years now. They have asked that there be a quick procedure, one that would deal with claims in the course of, say, five or six months.
In this Bill we are studying today, which has been before Parliament for the past year, the Government has not provided such a procedure. It has set up a screening procedure whereby only certain persons will be eligible for claims. Only persons who pass through what are known as safe third countries will not be eligible to have their claims determined in Canada. Therefore, we have had estimates over the course of the past few months which have been made public. We see that as many as 75 per cent, 80 per cent or even 90 per cent of claimants who come to Canada will not be eligible to have their claims determined under this legislation. The Government is really reneging on the only responsibility it has under the Geneva Convention of 1951, which is to determine on the merits the claims of people who claim to be refugees. Therefore, this Government risks and inevitably will send people who are refugees to persecution and even death because there is no procedure to permit the Government to determine who is or who is not a refugee.
I have another word or two about Canada's role, Mr. Speaker. I believe we have a special responsibility. We are a huge country with a small population. If not Canada, I put the question to the Parliamentary Secretary: "Which country will continue to provide a haven for refugees?" Which country will uphold the principles of the Geneva Convention?
If we in Canada cannot find it within ourselves to respect the rules of the Geneva Convention, will any other country in the world do so? Will other countries be justified in saying that if Canada will not respect the Geneva Convention, why should they? Costa Rica has a large number of refugees, as does West Germany and France, what will they say? I read about Italy the other day. There are perhaps one million refugee claimants who have flocked there from all parts of the world. What will the Italians say if Canada passes this legislation? Countries are going to refuse to let anybody enter because, if Canada cannot accept refugees with its wealth, its resources and small population, why should they?
I would like to remind the Parliamentary Secretary and Members of this House that our so-called refugee problem is very small in comparison to that which exists in many parts of the world. I come back to this because I believe the Member was engaging in a bit of fear-mongering when he referred to the billions of people. Over the past couple of years we have had perhaps 18,000, 19,000, or 20,000 claimants who have arrived on our shores. That might seem like a large number. But think about it, Mr. Speaker, you could fill one hockey arena with 19,000 or 20,000 claimants. It is not exactly an overwhelming number. Compare that to a tiny country like Costa Rica which has several hundred thousand claimants on
June 10, 1988

its territory, refugees who are seeking protection and who have sought safe haven there. Costa Rica has not sought to turn those refugees back. It has not closed its border to refugee claimants. What about Pakistan? There are 2 million or 3 million Afghans on Pakistan territory. Plow can Canada compare itself to a country like that?
I can only conclude by saying that this Government has not in its amendments dealt with the principal objections to this legislation. It has not dealt with its major flaws. This legislation is not worthy of our country. It not worthy to become the law of the land. If it does, unfortunately, at some point become the law of this land, I hope Canadians will turf out the Government so that a more responsible Government can amend it before any great damage is done.
